solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Suggesting my words are false introduces pressure

parts.note: what the speaker would say: I'M LYING
P = pressure, set between I'M and LYING

explanation.surface: Someone owning up that what they say is a sham, under pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a paraphrase to be turned back into speech: 'my words are false' is a confession you would say aloud in the first person.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: implying means suggesting something without stating it outright.

clue.text: Entertainer accepting a dodgy role on stage

explanation.surface: A performer taking on a shady character in a play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duff' is British slang for faulty or useless, which is what 'dodgy' means here.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Macduff, the thane who kills Macbeth, is one part in Shakespeare's play.

clue.text: Athlete ably running in set places

indicators.note: letters that are running about are loose and moving, so they settle in a new order

explanation.surface: A runner competing well in set positions on a track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Running' looks like the athlete's event, and 'set places' like starting blocks; both belong to the dining room instead.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: setting places, the cutlery and plates for each diner, is what laying the table means.

clue.text: Youngster losing head hands round drug, one unlikely to work

indicators.note: 'losing head' cuts a letter off
to go round something is to surround it

parts.note: E = ecstasy, held between L and R

explanation.surface: A decapitated youngster passing drugs around: a dark crime picture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hands' is not a verb here: it is the pair of hands, left and right, which wrap round the drug.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive paraphrase: an idler is lazy, and so someone unlikely to do any work.

clue.text: Socialist Party in summer time uprising

indicators.note: rising up, which in a down clue means the letters read from bottom to top
one thing in another is inside it

parts.note: a rave is a party, placed inside AUG: ARAVEUG

explanation.surface: A left-wing party staging a revolt in the summer.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's politics are real: Che Guevara led revolutions, so 'uprising' fits both the scene and the direction of reading.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Che Guevara, the Argentine Marxist revolutionary, is one famous socialist.

clue.text: Revolutionary has fun pets

indicators.note: a revolution is a turn right round, so the word is turned to read backwards

explanation.surface: A rebel enjoying the company of animals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pets' are not animals but sulks, as in 'in a pet'; a strop is British slang for a bad-tempered sulk.
explanation.definitionFit: A less common sense: a pet is a fit of sulking, which in British slang is a strop.

clue.text: Game is fine, with Reds put in new positions on the wings

indicators.note: on the wings means the rearranged letters sit on both sides of the other piece
in new positions means the letters of these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A football manager says it is fine to move the Reds players out to the wings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reds' suggests footballers, but the word simply joins 'put' as letters to be shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Stud poker is a card game in which some cards are dealt face up.

clue.text: Half-hearted, cross staff

indicators.note: with only half a heart, so the double-O middle keeps just one O

parts.note: a rood is a cross, especially in a church

explanation.surface: Grumpy staff who can't be bothered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like an adjective next to 'Half-hearted'; it is the noun, the old word rood.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a staff is a long stick, which is a rod.

clue.text: Sign nothing's missing in substandard holiday accommodation

indicators.note: something missing is absent

explanation.surface: A complaint that there's nothing laid on in a shabby campsite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sign' reads as a noticeboard at the campsite; it is an omen.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a portent is a sign or omen of something to come.

clue.text: Ruler favouring the Tories crows, stifling unknown protest forcefully

indicators.note: to stifle is to smother, so the chain closes over the unknown

parts.note: a murder of crows is the collective noun

explanation.surface: A Conservative-leaning monarch gloating while silencing an anonymous critic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crows' reads as a verb, gloats; it is the birds. Tories are the British Conservatives, whose party colour is blue.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: to cry blue murder is to make a loud, outraged fuss, a forceful protest.

clue.text: Retailer's opening guide for one making a career

indicators.note: a word's opening is where it starts, its first letter

parts.note: an usher guides people to seats

explanation.surface: A shop's starter manual for someone building a working life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Career' here is the verb, to rush headlong, not a profession.
explanation.definitionFit: A less common sense: to career is to hurtle along, so one making a career is a rusher.

clue.text: They may hold drugs from ace smugglers smuggling a lot of marijuana

parts.note: an ace in cards counts as one, written A

indicators.note: smuggling means carrying something hidden inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: mules are people who smuggle drugs across borders

indicators.note: a lot of, but not all, so the final letter of the slang word is dropped

explanation.surface: A tale of drug mules carrying cannabis across a border.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drugs' tempts you to the cannabis itself; the definition is the containers, and a mule is slang for a drug courier.
explanation.definitionFit: Ampoules are small sealed glass vials used to hold injectable medicines.

clue.text: Account not meriting credit or PIN in refined neighbourhood's banks

indicators.note: one thing in another is inside it

parts.note: pins = legs, informally; LEG goes before URBANE's last E

indicators.note: a river's banks are its two edges, so only the first and last letters count

parts.note: first and last letters of neighbourhood

explanation.surface: Banking jargon: an account refused credit, or a PIN problem at the posh local bank.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals of PIN point to a card number, but it is a leg, as in 'shaky on his pins'. 'Credit' means belief, not a loan.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: an urban legend is a story widely told but not worth believing.

clue.text: Wide, rotten boat full of animals covers miles

indicators.note: to cover something is to go over and round it

explanation.surface: A leaky, overloaded vessel spread over miles of water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wide' looks like a size for the boat; it is the adjective for a missed shot or a bowl that strays from its target.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a shot that goes wide misses its target, so it is off the mark.

clue.text: Pernod drunk hot and cool? It makes you feel good

indicators.note: drunk means the letters are befuddled into a new order

parts.note: H is the tap abbreviation for hot

explanation.surface: A glass of Pernod is hot and cool, and lifts your mood.
explanation.walkthrough: Pernod is a French aniseed spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: Endorphins are hormones released in the brain that bring a sense of wellbeing.

clue.text: It holds large quantity of alcohol still ultimately doubled

definitions.text: It holds large quantity of alcohol

indicators.note: ultimately doubled means its last letter is written twice

parts.note: still in the sense of nevertheless means but

explanation.surface: A vessel holding plenty of drink, with the still's output doubled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'still' looks like a distilling vessel, but here it means nevertheless.
explanation.definitionFit: A butt is a large cask for wine or beer.

clue.text: Go nuts, giving a twirl

indicators.note: a twirl spins something right round, so the word ends up backwards

explanation.surface: A dancer going wild with a spin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go nuts' reads as one phrase, to go crazy; split it, and 'Go' is the definition, as in 'have a go'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a go at something is an attempt, and so is a stab at it.

clue.text: He leaves the lecture in an emotional state

indicators.note: someone who leaves goes away, so HE departs from the letters

explanation.surface: A man walking out of a talk, overcome with feeling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He' is not the man in the scene but the two letters, taken out of 'the'.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive paraphrase: tearful means close to crying, one particular emotional state.

clue.text: Hack off lizard's tail with inarticulate sound? Man perhaps admits it

indicators.note: a tail is the end of an animal, so the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Chopping off a lizard's tail, and a man grunting about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' is not a person but the Isle of Man, between Britain and Ireland. 'Hack off' is British slang for annoy.
explanation.definitionFit: A regional idiom: in British slang to hack someone off is to annoy them, to disgruntle them.

clue.text: Someone who sells fish turned over a kipper?

indicators.note: something turned over is flipped end to end, so the chain reads backwards

explanation.surface: A fishmonger flipping a smoked herring.
explanation.walkthrough: A kipper is a smoked herring, which fits the fishmonger; the definition means one who kips.
explanation.definitionFit: A pun on a regional word: to kip is British slang for to sleep, so a kipper is a sleeper.

clue.text: 50 old songs played at gig coming up, including It's Not Unusual?

indicators.note: including means the outer letters take in the other piece

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for 50

indicators.note: coming up in a down clue means the letters are read from bottom to top

parts.note: a set is the list of songs a band plays at a gig

explanation.surface: An oldies band plays a set at a gig, including Tom Jones's hit It's Not Unusual.
explanation.walkthrough: It's Not Unusual is a 1965 Tom Jones hit, but the title is split: 'It' goes into the wordplay and 'Not Unusual?' is the example defining the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Litotes is understatement by negating the opposite, as saying 'not unusual' for common.

clue.text: Sunny capital of Eritrea maybe pedestrianised around the outside

indicators.note: placed round the outside of something
a capital is an upper-case letter, and a word's capital is its first letter

explanation.surface: A travel note: the Eritrean capital with its sunny, pedestrian-only streets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital of Eritrea' sends you to Asmara; it is only the capital letter E.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for a temperament: a sunny, cheerful person is carefree.

clue.text: As yet struggling to dress wife covered in beads

indicators.note: to dress means to clothe, so these letters wrap around the other piece
struggling means the letters writhe into a new order

explanation.surface: A struggle to get the wife dressed, while sweat pours.
explanation.definitionFit: Beads of sweat on the skin mean someone is sweaty, perspiring heavily.

clue.text: What's up with album's mindless followers?

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: an EP is a short record; the 's is 'has', joining it to the definition

explanation.surface: Asking what's happening with a band's brainless fans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What's up' reads as a greeting, but it is the word 'what's' written upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A figurative use: people who follow the crowd without thinking are called sheep.

clue.text: Scottish runner offering to conserve energy now

indicators.note: to conserve is to keep safe inside

parts.note: the River Forth, which flows past Edinburgh
a present = a gift, an offering
E = energy, held between the two

explanation.surface: A Scottish athlete promising to save strength for later.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'runner' is a river, a crossword staple: the Forth is a Scottish river.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: for the present means for the time being, as things stand now.

clue.text: Soldiers see gun

explanation.surface: An order to troops to look at a weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gun' is not the weapon but the verb, as in gunning an engine.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb sense: gunning an engine means pressing the accelerator hard, the same as revving it.

clue.text: On vacation, Croatian houses dear in Split

indicators.note: a place on vacation is vacated, emptied of its middle

parts.note: love and dear are both terms of endearment

explanation.surface: Holiday lettings: Croatian homes for rent in Split.
explanation.walkthrough: Split is the Croatian port, which the surface sets up perfectly; the definition is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: cloven is the old past participle of cleave, so split, as in a cloven hoof.

clue.text: Sort of music that is at a higher tempo than the rest

definitions.text: at a higher tempo than the rest

explanation.surface: A remark about a style of music played faster than all others.
explanation.walkthrough: The tempo talk keeps the music going, but the definition describes the answer, not the genre.
explanation.definitionFit: A superlative paraphrase: rapidest means fastest of all, going quicker than every other.
